claims.text: Substrate-induced residual stresses govern the magnetocaloric response of nanoscale non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films or nanoribbons under low-field cooling cycles.
Substrate-induced residual stresses govern the hysteresis associated with low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Residual stresses modulate local magnetic ordering and magnetic phase-transition dynamics.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons have significant residual stress.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons contain quenched-in defects.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons possess a disordered magnetic microstructure.
Controlled post-deposition thermal annealing can partially relax substrate-induced residual stress without significant grain growth or phase segregation.
Residual microstrain and grain-boundary defects affect magnetic-domain evolution.
Residual microstrain and grain-boundary defects affect the kinetics of the magnetic phase transition.
Annealing-induced stress relaxation reduces microstructural and magnetic inhomogeneity.
Reduced inhomogeneity produces a more uniform magnetic-domain structure.
Stress relaxation and improved magnetic uniformity sharpen the magnetic transition.
A sharper magnetic transition enhances the low-field magnetocaloric response.
Stress relaxation and improved magnetic uniformity suppress extrinsic hysteresis.
Annealed samples will exhibit a larger adiabatic temperature change or magnetic entropy change than the as-deposited baseline under low applied fields.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower hysteresis losses than the as-deposited baseline during cooling cycles.
Heat transfer across the nanoscale film-substrate interface caps the effective magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
As-deposited films have broadened magnetic transitions and significant hysteresis because of uneven stress distributions and defects.
The predicted annealing effect is confined primarily to a narrow temperature interval around the magnetic transition and to applied fields of tens to a few hundred millitesla.
At higher fields or at temperatures far from the magnetic transition, factors other than stress-induced defects may dominate the response.
